subjects.displayTitle: The power of the Manifestation: a world made new
subjects.introduction: What kind of power can be expressed through captivity, bodily weakness and a willingness to suffer for the freedom of others? These readings invite that question before they unfold their language of sovereignty, creative utterance and the renewal of the world. The Manifestation appears as a divine Educator whose influence reaches into character, understanding and the relationships among peoples; images of sunlight, a cultivated garden and latent warmth describe capacities brought to life. Claims of miraculous power stand beside careful distinctions about what reported wonders can prove, what scriptural images may mean, and why inward sight and enduring life matter. The collection also holds together declarations of authority and accounts of forbearance, hidden splendor and a response that cannot simply be compelled. Its letters, prayers, explanations and recollections speak from different settings, and their attributions help keep those voices distinct. The neighboring subjects of the Manifestation’s station, the voice of Divinity, divine omnipotence and the Word of God invite a closer reading of the relationship between the human person and divine revelation. John’s prologue and the encounter of Jesus with Pilate offer further occasions to examine life, recognition and sovereignty. As the sequence returns to service and remembrance, the question becomes personal: what would it mean for the power described here to bear fruit in the way we learn, act and live with one another?
subjects.arc: Power that gives life → The fruits of education → Miracles, evidence and recognition → The station of the divine Educator → A word that renews creation → The promise and the voice → Capacity, veils and the act of seeing → Sovereignty and its purpose → The call from within captivity → Encounters and recollections → An influence that continues → Receiving power through service → Further supplied readings

questions: What changes in your understanding of power when the guide begins with sorrow accepted for others’ joy and imprisonment accepted for their liberation? Which later passage most deepens or complicates that opening?
What kinds of transformation do the readings attribute to spiritual education—in a person, a relationship or a community? How might one distinguish an enduring fruit from an impressive appearance?

How do the passages distinguish the possibility of miracles, the reliability of a reported event, and the meaning of a scriptural image? What forms of inquiry become possible when those questions are considered separately?

How do the images of sun, mirror, Word, ocean and divine command work alongside explanations of the Manifestations’ stations? Where does an image help understanding, and where might taking it too simply obscure a distinction?
How are human receptivity, effort and service related to the power described here? What do the passages about withheld splendor and future Manifestations suggest about the limits of our expectations?

What becomes clearer when these readings are placed beside John’s accounts of the Word and of Jesus before Pilate? Which connected subject—the station of the Manifestation, the voice of Divinity, the Word of God or divine omnipotence—would help you pursue an unresolved question?

references.label: 1 · John 18:33–38 · Sovereignty before a ruler
references.note: In this exchange with Pilate, Jesus speaks of a kingdom whose source is beyond the world and connects His coming with witness to truth. He explains that His servants would fight if His kingdom were of this world. Read the exchange beside the passages that describe spiritual sovereignty amid captivity and affirm a purpose of education and liberation. How does each text ask the reader to recognize power? What follows when hearing truth, rather than commanding armed protection, occupies the center of an account of kingship? The Gospel’s particular narrative and the Bahá’í passages illuminate one another without making their settings identical.
references.verified: Read John 18:33–38 in full in the King James Version on Bible Gateway on 2026-10-10; verified the questions, the kingdom’s source, the reference to servants fighting, witness to truth and Pilate’s response.

references.label: 2 · John 1:1–18 · The Word, life and recognition
references.note: Read the prologue as a whole around the supplied quotation from verse 14. It connects the Word with creation, life and light, yet also describes a world that fails to recognize its source. Compare this tension with the compilation’s language of creative utterance and the veils that hinder recognition. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s explanation of the Manifestations’ three stations offers a further point of comparison. Where do the texts use similar images, and what does each actually say about divine presence and human life? Shared vocabulary can invite careful inquiry while leaving distinct theological meanings open to examination.
